The tiny beachfront community of Gilchrist was completely swept away, save for only a few homes; one home remained intact though rendered uninhabitable.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Kemah, Texas, about 35 miles (56 km) south of Houston, was without power and water, and still had 5 feet of flooding on Saturday, September 13, 2008. Severe damage occurred at the Kemah Boardwalk, the site of many popular restaurants and shops, as well as a small waterfront amusement park. The entire first floor of Landry's seafood restaurant was demolished and swept away, as well as those of neighboring structures.

In Seabrook, most homes and businesses east of State Highway 146 (close to Galveston Bay) were flooded by storm surge, which included the Miramar subdivision and 'Old Seabrook'. Homes along Todville Rd were washed away, or had their entire bottom floors gutted. State Highway 146 just north of the Kemah Bridge was completely inundated, causing boats and other debris to collect on the highway. The Seabrook Waterfront district sustained substantial damage. The surge caused boats to float onto or very close to Nasa Road 1, and also destroyed boat docks and businesses along Nasa Road 1 all the way to the Nassau Bay Hilton hotel.

Later, the remnants redeveloped into a tropical storm just off the coast of the Mexican state of Campeche, and the storm made a subsequent landfall near Naples, Florida (United States). Finally, former Hurricane Mitch passed north of Scotland.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system evolved from a tropical depression into Tropical Storm Mitch and then became a hurricane on October 24, displaying the classic evolution of a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: At peak intensity, Mitch maintained maximum sustained winds of 180 mph (290 km/h), indicating that high winds were the primary hazard associated with this event.

Event_Names: Effects of the 1919 Florida Keys hurricane in Texas
Time_Annotation: The storm originated from the Leeward Islands early in September 1919 and took a generally west-northwestward course, devastating the Florida Keys en route to the Gulf of Mexico. On the afternoon of September 14, the center of the hurricane made landfall upon the Texas coast at Baffin Bay. After slowly moving ashore, it weakened and straddled the Rio Grande before dissipating on September 16 over West Texas.

Time_Annotation: The tropical wave that became Dennis was identified by the National Hurricane Center on June 26, 2005, well inland over Africa; Dennis' remnant circulation dissipated over Ontario on July 18, 2005.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The depression soon crossed the island country of Grenada before entering the Caribbean; the powerful storm struck the western tip of Granma Province, Cuba; it made landfall over Santa Rosa Island in Florida (USA) as the hurricane approached the Florida Panhandle; and its remnant circulation traversed the river valleys of the Mississippi and Ohio before finally dissipating over Ontario (Canada).
Main_Event_Annotation: Turning west-northwest, the system achieved tropical storm status on July 5 and hurricane status the following day, clearly placing it in the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm intensified with peak winds of 150 miles per hour (240 km/h) before weakening due to an eyewall replacement cycle, indicating wind as the primary hazard.
